Masrekah
MAS-ruh-kah
proper noun
Hebrew Masreqah, from a root soreq for the choice vine, hence “place of the noble vine” or “vineyard”; the home city of Samlah, king of Edom.

Biblical Definition

Masrekah is a name we should never have known but that the Spirit of God saw fit to write it: “And Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his stead” (Gen 36:36). A single verse, a single king, a city otherwise lost to all memory — and yet the Holy Ghost recorded it. Why should the inspired page trouble itself with the petty thrones of Edom, the reprobate line of Esau? Because the God who chose Jacob is sovereign over Esau also. He numbers the kings of the cast-away no less than the kings of the covenant; not a duke of Edom rises but by His decree, not one dies but in His appointed hour. The doctrine of election is no mere favoritism; it is the rule of the Most High over both vessels, the vessel of mercy and the vessel of wrath. Samlah of Masrekah reigned because God ordained his little day, and passed because God had numbered it. Herein is comfort: the same hand that governs the throne of the wicked upholds the least of His saints. If the LORD keeps a book of Edom's forgotten kings, how much more are the names of His people graven in the Lamb's book of life. Masrekah, the place of the choice vine, reminds us that nothing is too small for providence, and no crown too great to escape it.

Webster 1828 Definition

The home city of Samlah, king of Edom (Gen 36:36); a witness that God is sovereign over the reprobate line of Esau as well as the elect line of Jacob.

expand to see more

MASREKAH, the city of Samlah, king of Edom.

Named once only: “Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his stead” (Gen 36:36).

The name means the place of the choice or noble vine.

Recorded by the Spirit though it is a throne of the reprobate line.

A token that God rules over Esau's kings as over Jacob's.

Key Scripture

Gen 36:36 — "And Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his stead."

1Ch 1:43 — "Now these are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the children of Israel; Bela the son of Beor: and the name of his city was Dinhabah."

Rev 20:12 — "And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works."

Heb 11:16 — "But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city."

Modern Corruption

The city of Samlah, an Edomite king recorded in a single verse; it recovers the sovereignty of God over the reprobate line no less than the elect.

expand to see more

An Edomite town named once stirs no modern controversy. Its worth is doctrinal: that the Spirit troubled to record the thrones of Esau's line at all testifies that God governs the cast-away as truly as the chosen.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the universal reach of providence and election. The God who numbered Samlah's little reign numbers the hairs of His people's heads. If He keeps a book of Edom's forgotten kings, the names of His elect are surely safe in the Lamb's book of life.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Masreqah, from soreq, the choice vine; the seat of King Samlah of Edom.

expand to see more

Masrekah — the home city of Samlah (Gen 36:36).

The root soreq denotes a choice or noble vine.

Hence the sense “place of the vineyard.”

The fifth-named king in the Edomite roll of Genesis 36.

A name preserved by inspiration though the throne was reprobate.

Usage

"Samlah of Masrekah reigned after Hadad in Edom."

"Masrekah, the place of the choice vine, is named but once."

"Even Masrekah's forgotten king was under God's decree."
